symptoms: First signs are white to grey-green spots with dark green borders.
Older spots are elliptical or spindle-shaped, whitish to grey, with a dead border.
Some spots are diamond-shaped: wide in the middle and pointed at both ends.
Spots can grow and merge until the whole leaf dies.
treatment: Systemic fungicides such as triazoles and strobilurins can be used, with care.
A fungicide application at heading can control the disease.
prevention: Sow early, soon after the rainy season starts.
Split nitrogen fertiliser into several applications and avoid excess.
Keep the field flooded as often as possible.
Silicon fertiliser can reduce blast; if straw is used as the silicon source, it must be free of blast.
rice___Blast.severity: Severe leaf blast reduces grain yield.

symptoms: Seedlings show small, circular, yellow-brown or brown spots.
Spots on leaves later turn dark brown to purple-brown.
Fully developed spots are circular to oval with a light brown to grey centre and a reddish-brown edge.
treatment: Improve soil fertility: check soil nutrients and apply the fertilisers that are needed.
Fungicides such as iprodione, propiconazole and azoxystrobin are used as seed treatments.
prevention: Monitor soil nutrients regularly and keep the soil fertile.
On soils low in silicon, apply calcium silicate slag before planting.
Treat seed with hot water before planting to control infection carried on the seed.
rice___Brown_spot.severity: The many large spots can kill the whole leaf, and infection leads to poorly filled, lower quality grain.

sources.title: Brown spot, IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank

symptoms: Leaves wilt and turn yellow; seedlings may wilt completely (called kresek).
On seedlings, infected leaves turn greyish green and roll up.
As the disease progresses, leaves turn yellow to straw-coloured and wilt, and whole seedlings dry up and die.
treatment: Use balanced amounts of plant nutrients, especially nitrogen.
Make sure fields and nurseries drain well.
Keep fields clean: remove weed hosts and plough under rice stubble, straw, ratoons and volunteer seedlings, which can host the bacteria.
prevention: Let fallow fields dry out to suppress the bacteria in the soil and plant residues.
Keep fields free of weeds and of stubble from infected plants.
rice___Bacterial_blight.severity: Yield loss can be as much as 70% when susceptible varieties are grown in conditions that favour the disease.

sources.title: Bacterial blight, IRRI Rice Knowledge Bank

symptoms: Plants are stunted and have fewer tillers.
Grains are sterile or only partly filled, sometimes with dark brown blotches.
treatment: Remove infected plants to limit the spread of the virus.
Insecticides are often ineffective, because leafhoppers move between fields.
prevention: Grow varieties resistant to tungro or to leafhoppers.
Plant at the same time as the surrounding farms.
Time planting for when leafhopper numbers are low.
Plough infected stubble under straight after harvest.
Do not use seedlings from nurseries in areas where tungro is common.
rice___Tungro.severity: One of the most destructive rice diseases in South and Southeast Asia; in severe cases yield loss can reach 100%.
